plan.contextChunk: This figure traces the operation of merge sort on an eight-element array as a bottom-up lattice of gray boxes linked by thick gray arrows. The bottom rank, tagged "initial sequence", holds eight single-element squares reading 5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 2, 6 from left to right. Pairs of arrows, each pair captioned "merge", lift adjacent squares into four two-element boxes reading 2 5, 4 7, 1 3, and 2 6. A second rank of merge arrows combines those into two four-element boxes, 2 4 5 7 and 1 2 3 6. A last pair of arrows, again captioned "merge", brings both into the wide box at the top, tagged "sorted sequence", which reads 1 2 2 3 4 5 6 7. Box width scales with the run it holds, so the doubling of sorted-run length shows up directly as the boxes widen from rank to rank while their count halves. Read upward, the drawing presents the algorithm as repeated merging of already-sorted runs.

interactionPlan.concept: Merge sort works bottom-up as one repeated operation — merging two already-sorted runs into one longer sorted run — applied at every level from singletons up to the final sequence.
elements: top label 'sorted sequence'
top wide box, 8 cells reading 1 2 2 3 4 5 6 7
two level-2 boxes reading 2 4 5 7 (left) and 1 2 3 6 (right)
four level-1 boxes reading 2 5, 4 7, 1 3, 2 6 (left to right)
eight singleton boxes reading 5, 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 2, 6 (left to right)
bottom label 'initial sequence'
thick gray arrow pairs linking adjacent child boxes to their parent box at each level
'merge' captions beside each arrow pair (three levels)
cell divider lines in every multi-element box
subscripts tagging the duplicate 2 values (visible when the stability trace is on)

interactions.label: Implement merge(left, right)

api.does: read the front (first not-yet-taken) value of run 'left' or 'right'; undefined when that run is empty
true once every value in that run has been taken
compare two values — choosing <= over < is exactly what decides what happens on ties
append the front value of that run to the output box — the ONLY way to build the sorted result
drop a text marker on the current frame, shown in the replay trace

interactions.frame: the two active runs and the partially filled output box, with a pointer on each run's front element and the next output slot highlighted
interactions.success_check: the output contains all values in non-decreasing order, AND for equal front values the left run's copy is taken before the right run's copy (the merge is stable)
interactions.teaches: Merging two sorted runs is a front-pointer procedure: compare the two fronts, take the smaller (left copy on ties), and repeat — the replay shows exactly in what order values enter the output and why

interactions.label: Active merge tier
interactions.teaches: Every level of the tree does the same merge work on runs twice as long and half as many — the doubling of run length versus halving of run count is the source of the n log n running time

interactions.label: Stability trace
interactions.teaches: Tagging the two duplicate 2s shows merge never inverts their relative order — taking the left run's copy on ties is what makes merge sort stable, not an accident of the data

demo_steps.title: Read the lattice bottom-up
demo_steps.narration: Eight singletons merge into four sorted pairs, then two sorted quads, then one sorted sequence. Box width scales with run length, so each tier doubles the sorted-run size and halves the run count.

demo_steps.title: Write the merge routine
demo_steps.narration: The active pair and destination highlight at the final tier. Implement merge(left, right) with the front/isEmpty/take primitives and watch the replay fill the output box one comparison at a time — this one routine is the whole algorithm.

demo_steps.title: Prove stability on the 2s
demo_steps.narration: Turn on the stability trace and rerun: the two 2s stay in their original left-then-right order only if ties resolve toward the left run. Swap <= for < and the trace shows the order flip while the values still look sorted.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Merge sort does exactly one thing — merge two already-sorted runs, front by front — and applies it at log n levels where total work per level is n; the only subtlety is that ties must favor the left run to keep the sort stable.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Serif textbook styling on white. Five horizontal ranks: eight single-cell gray boxes at the bottom under the label 'initial sequence'; four two-cell gray boxes above; two four-cell gray boxes above those; one eight-cell gray box at top under the label 'sorted sequence'. Box width scales with the number of cells so doubling reads visually. Cells are light gray with thin black borders and black dividers; values centered in each cell. Thick gray arrows rise from each pair of child boxes up to their parent box, with the italic word 'merge' between each arrow pair. Highlight the active tier by dimming all other ranks. When the stability trace is on, mark the two cells containing 2 (one in the third singleton/second quad box, one in the fourth singleton... i.e. the duplicate 2s in the left and right runs) with small colored subscript tags 2-and-2 that persist through merge levels so their relative order stays observable.

Figure 2.4 illustrates the operation of the procedure bottom-up when n is a power of 2. The algorithm consists of merging pairs of 1-item sequences to form sorted sequences of length 2, merging pairs of sequences of length 2 to form sorted sequences of length 4, and so on, until two sequences of length n=2 are merged to form the final sorted sequence of length n.

discrepancies: In the default step-0 state, the upper three tiers are faded to near-invisibility and the tier-2/3 arrows and 'merge' captions are barely visible, whereas the source figure presents all four tiers fully and uniformly
The node boxes use a very light gray (#e7e7e7) versus the source's slightly darker gray fill, a minor color difference
The arrows in the source are thick gray arrows in every tier with consistent 'merge' labels between each pair; in the default view only the bottom tier's arrows are rendered at full opacity
The source shows the 'sorted sequence' label directly above the top row; in the generated figure the faded top tier makes this label-to-row association weak at first glance
evaluation.notes: All four tiers, correct values, node topology, and labels match the source, with the dimming of inactive tiers being an intentional (if slightly fidelity-reducing) interactive device; the interactions (tier selection, stability trace, runnable code-editor merge workbench with replay) are extensive and conceptually on-target.
action_items: Raise the dimmed-tier opacity (e.g. DIM_LV from 0.32 to ~0.55 and DIM_AR from 0.12 to ~0.35) so the full lattice remains clearly recognizable in the default state
Darken the cell fill from #e7e7e7 toward the source's medium gray for closer color match
Consider auto-running the sample merge during demo step 2 so the highlight/replay affordance is visible without requiring the user to click 'Run merge'
